title: Relocate Marbles
statement:
Marbles sit on a number line; `nums` lists the position of each marble (several marbles may share a position). The arrays `moveFrom` and `moveTo` have the same length and describe moves applied in order: move `i` picks up every marble currently at position `moveFrom[i]` and puts all of them at position `moveTo[i]`. Each move is guaranteed to find at least one marble at `moveFrom[i]`, and `moveFrom[i]` may equal `moveTo[i]`.

After every move has been applied, return the positions that hold at least one marble, each listed once, in increasing order.
constraints: When move i is applied, at least one marble is at position moveFrom[i]
signature: List<Integer> relocateMarbles(int[] nums, int[] moveFrom, int[] moveTo)
notes:
## Intuition

The answer only asks which positions are occupied, not how many marbles sit there. A move empties its source completely and makes its target occupied, whatever the counts were. So a set of occupied positions is enough: each move is one removal and one insertion. Simulating each marble separately also works but costs O(n·m).

## Approach

1. Put every starting position from `nums` into the set `occupied` (duplicates collapse).
2. For each move `i`, delete `moveFrom[i]` from `occupied`, then add `moveTo[i]`.
3. Copy the set into `result`, sort it numerically and return it.

Deleting before adding matters when `moveFrom[i] === moveTo[i]`: the marbles stay put and the position must remain in the set.

## Example 1, step by step

`occupied` starts as `{1, 6, 7, 8}`. Move 0 deletes 1 and adds 2: `{6, 7, 8, 2}`. Move 1 deletes 7 and adds 9: `{6, 8, 2, 9}`. Move 2 deletes 2 and adds 5: `{6, 8, 9, 5}`. Sorting gives `[5, 6, 8, 9]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m + k log k): building the set and applying the `m` moves are constant time per step, and the `k` final positions are sorted once.
- Space: O(n + m): the set holds at most the starting positions plus one new position per move.

## Pitfalls

- Adding before deleting erases the position when a move's source and target are the same.
- Sort with `(a, b) => a - b`; the default sort compares numbers as text, so `10` would come before `9`.
- Return each occupied position once, even when many marbles end up there.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `occupied` | set of positions holding at least one marble |
| `i` | index of the move being applied |
| `result` | the occupied positions in increasing order |

narration.2: Collect the starting positions; several marbles at one spot count once.
narration.3: Apply the moves one at a time, in order.
narration.4: Every marble leaves the source, so it is no longer occupied.
narration.5: They all land on the target, which is now occupied (re-adding it covers a move onto itself).
narration.7: Copy the occupied positions into an array.
narration.8: Sort numerically so the positions come out in increasing order.
